bracket: [Textbook misprint in the answer key: part (c) is printed as \(3.0 \times 10^{-23}\,\text{m}\), which is too large by a factor of \(100\) — the de Broglie wavelength of the dust particle is \(3.0 \times 10^{-25}\,\text{m}\). Parts (a) and (b) are printed correctly, and they are what settle it: the key's own (b) gives \(\lambda = 1.1 \times 10^{-32}\,\text{m}\) at \(p = 0.060\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\), i.e. \(h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s}\), and that same \(h\) at \(p = 2.2 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\) returns exactly \(3.0 \times 10^{-25}\,\text{m}\) — reproducing the key's own mantissa \(3.0\) with only the exponent differing. A mass of \(1.005 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{kg}\) would be needed to make \(3.0 \times 10^{-23}\,\text{m}\) correct, two decades away from the \(1.0 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{kg}\) the question states. Only the exponent is broken; the method and the mantissa the book prints are right.]
